title: Tutorial on large scale optimisation: II
html:
In the last post we have developed background and basic algorithms such as forward-backward splitting and Douglas-Rachford splitting in large scale optimisation, where ADMM is a equivalent to applying the D-R splitting to the dual decomposition. The proof of convergence of the D-R splitting was delayed until this post.

Here we will systematically develop a general convergence analysis framework, which will include almost all the algorithms we have seen so far:

  • Gradient descent;
  • Basic proximal point method (which is equivalent to applying gradient descent to the Moreau-Yosida envelope);
  • Forward-backward splitting;
  • Douglas-Rachford splitting.

As you will see, once the machinery is developed, all the convergence proofs are really a one-line argument, and is in some sense ultimately from gradient descent!

A standard reference here I guess is prof. Combettes' Solving Monotone Inclusions via Compositions of Nonexpansive averaged operator. My notes here are again combination of various (well known) sources, but I found prof. Giselsson's graphical representations in his lecture notes to be extremely helpful in succinctly express all the essential ideas. But these ideas may not be clear from a first read of my post and I only took two figures from his lectures, so interested readers please go to the original source for a more detailed exposition.

Before we start this abstract topic, let's recall what we have last time and take a few concrete examples at the implementation level.

1. Examples of implementation of ADMM

In the last post we derived the ADMM algorithm from the Douglas-Rachford splitting. Recall that the ADMM algorithm for the problem

min⁡x∈Rd1,y∈Rd2  f1(x)+f2(y)subject toAx+By=b(1) \displaystyle \begin{aligned} &\min_{\substack{x\in \mathbb{R}^{d_1}, y\in \mathbb{R}^{d_2}}} \; & & f_1(x) + f_2(y)\\ & \text{subject to} & & Ax + By = b \end{aligned} (1)​x∈Rd1​,y∈Rd2​​min​subject to​​f1​(x)+f2​(y)Ax+By=b​(1)

with step size τ {\tau}τ, and initialisation s0,y0 {s^0, y^0}s0,y0, is the following iteration

xk+1=arg⁡min⁡xf1(x)+⟨sk,Ax⟩+12∥Ax+Byk−b∥2;yk+1=arg⁡min⁡yf2(y)+⟨sk,By⟩+12τ∥Axk+1+By−b∥2;sk+1=sk+Axk+1+Byk+1−bτ.\displaystyle \begin{aligned} x^{k+1} & = \arg\min_{x} f_1(x) + \langle s^k, Ax\rangle + \frac{1}{2}\| Ax + By^k - b\|^2; \\ y^{k+1} &= \arg\min_{y} f_2(y) + \langle s^k, By\rangle + \frac{1}{2\tau}\| Ax^{k+1} + By - b\|^2; \\ s^{k+1} &= s^k + \frac{Ax^{k+1} + By^{k+1} - b}{\tau}. \end{aligned}xk+1yk+1sk+1​=argxmin​f1​(x)+⟨sk,Ax⟩+21​∥Ax+Byk−b∥2;=argymin​f2​(y)+⟨sk,By⟩+2τ1​∥Axk+1+By−b∥2;=sk+τAxk+1+Byk+1−b​.​

The algorithm enjoys three convergence properties when the strong duality holds:

  • Residual convergence. The residuals Axk+Byk−b→0 {Ax^k+By^k-b \rightarrow 0}Axk+Byk−b→0, i.e. the iterates approach feasibility;
  • Primal value convergence. f1(xk)+f2(yk)→p∗ {f_1(x^k)+f_2(y^k)\rightarrow p^*}f1​(xk)+f2​(yk)→p∗, where p∗ {p^*}p∗ is the optimal value of the primal problem;
  • Dual variable convergence. The Lagrange multiplier sequence converge to the dual optimal point sk→s∗ {s^k\rightarrow s^*}sk→s∗.

The convergence properties, especially that the solution becomes feasible in the limit, together with the parallelisable iterations, makes ADMM very useful.
Before we proceed further, it might be better to see how it is actually implemented for various optimisation problems in applications. For convenience we want to rewrite the iteration a bit, sometimes called the scaled form of ADMM. Let ρ=1/τ {\rho = 1/\tau}ρ=1/τ, u=τs {u = \tau s}u=τs, and notice that

⟨sk,Ax+Byk−b⟩+12τ∥Ax+Byk−b∥2=ρ2∥Ax+Byk−b+u∥2−ρ2∥u∥2\displaystyle \langle s^k, Ax+By^k-b\rangle + \frac{1}{2\tau}\| Ax + By^k - b\|^2 = \frac{\rho}{2}\|Ax+By^k-b+u\|^2 -\frac{\rho}{2}\|u\|^2⟨sk,Ax+Byk−b⟩+2τ1​∥Ax+Byk−b∥2=2ρ​∥Ax+Byk−b+u∥2−2ρ​∥u∥2

and similarly for other terms. We find that the iteration is equivalent to

xk+1=arg⁡min⁡xf1(x)+ρ2∥Ax+Byk−b+uk∥2;yk+1=arg⁡min⁡yf2(y)+ρ2∥Axk+1+By−b+uk∥2;uk+1=uk+Axk+1+Byk+1−b.\displaystyle \begin{aligned} x^{k+1} & = \arg\min_{x} f_1(x) + \frac{\rho}{2}\| Ax + By^k - b + u^k\|^2; \\ y^{k+1} &= \arg\min_{y} f_2(y) + \frac{\rho}{2}\| Ax^{k+1} + By - b + u^k\|^2; \\ u^{k+1} &= u^k + Ax^{k+1} + By^{k+1} - b. \end{aligned}xk+1yk+1uk+1​=argxmin​f1​(x)+2ρ​∥Ax+Byk−b+uk∥2;=argymin​f2​(y)+2ρ​∥Axk+1+By−b+uk∥2;=uk+Axk+1+Byk+1−b.​

Note that uk {u^k}uk is basically a running sum of residuals. And in case A=B=±I {A=B=\pm I}A=B=±I, the x {x}x- and y {y}y- subproblems are proximal iterations.

Example 1 (Basis pursuit) The original problem is of the form

min⁡∥x∥1subject to Mx=c(2) \displaystyle \begin{aligned} &\min \|x\|_1 \\ &\text{subject to } Mx=c \end{aligned} (2)​min∥x∥1​subject to Mx=c​(2)

In order to apply ADMM, we can transform the problem into

min⁡∥x∥1+I{y:My=c}subject to x−y=0(3) \displaystyle \begin{aligned} &\min \|x\|_1 + I_{\{y:My=c\}} \\ &\text{subject to } x-y=0 \end{aligned} (3)​min∥x∥1​+I{y:My=c}​subject to x−y=0​(3)

The we can write down the x {x}x-subproblem, which is the familiar soft-thresholding

xk+1=arg⁡min⁡x∥x∥1+ρ2∥x−yk+uk∥2=soft-threshold(1/ρ,yk−uk):=(max⁡(0,∣yik−uik∣−1/ρ))i\displaystyle \begin{aligned} x^{k+1} & = \arg\min_{x} \|x\|_1 + \frac{\rho}{2}\| x - y^k + u^k\|^2 \\ & = \text{soft-threshold}(1/\rho, y^k - u^k) \\ & := (\max(0,|y^k_i - u^k_i| - 1/\rho))_i \end{aligned}xk+1​=argxmin​∥x∥1​+2ρ​∥x−yk+uk∥2=soft-threshold(1/ρ,yk−uk):=(max(0,∣yik​−uik​∣−1/ρ))i​​

and the y {y}y-subproblem is a projection to affine set

yk+1=arg⁡min⁡yI{y:My=q}+ρ2∥xk+1−y+uk∥2=proj{y:My=q}(xk+1+uk)=(I−MT(MMT)−1M)(xk+1+uk)−MT(MMT)−1c.\displaystyle \begin{aligned} y^{k+1} & = \arg\min_{y} I_{\{y:My=q\}} + \frac{\rho}{2}\| x^{k+1} - y + u^k\|^2 \\ & = \text{proj}_{\{y:My=q\}}(x^{k+1} + u^k) \\ & = (I-M^T(MM^T)^{-1}M)(x^{k+1} + u^k) - M^T(MM^T)^{-1}c. \end{aligned}yk+1​=argymin​I{y:My=q}​+2ρ​∥xk+1−y+uk∥2=proj{y:My=q}​(xk+1+uk)=(I−MT(MMT)−1M)(xk+1+uk)−MT(MMT)−1c.​

Example 2 (Lasso) The original problem is

min⁡μ2∥Mx−c∥2+∥x∥1(4) \displaystyle \min \frac{\mu}{2}\|Mx-c\|^2+\|x\|_1 (4)min2μ​∥Mx−c∥2+∥x∥1​(4)

Where μ>0 {\mu>0}μ>0 is a parameter. Then we do splitting by introducing a new variable y {y}y and reformulate the problem as

min⁡x,y12∥Mx−c∥2+λ∥y∥1subject to x−y=0(5) \displaystyle \begin{aligned} &\min_{x,y} \frac{1}{2}\|Mx-c\|^2+\lambda\|y\|_1 \\ &\text{subject to } x-y=0 \end{aligned} (5)​x,ymin​21​∥Mx−c∥2+λ∥y∥1​subject to x−y=0​(5)

Where λ>0 {\lambda>0}λ>0 is a parameter. Then the x {x}x-subproblem is a ridge regression, or Tikhonov regularisation on a quadratic problem

xk+1=arg⁡min⁡x12∥Mx−c∥2+ρ2∥x−yk+uk∥2=(MTM+ρI)−1(MTc+ρ(yk−uk))\displaystyle \begin{aligned} x^{k+1} &= \arg\min_x \frac{1}{2}\|Mx-c\|^2 + \frac{\rho}{2}\|x-y^k + u^k\|^2 \\ &= (M^TM+\rho I)^{-1}(M^Tc + \rho (y^k-u^k)) \end{aligned}xk+1​=argxmin​21​∥Mx−c∥2+2ρ​∥x−yk+uk∥2=(MTM+ρI)−1(MTc+ρ(yk−uk))​

The y {y}y-subproblem is the familiar soft-thresholding

yk+1=arg⁡min⁡yλ∥y∥1+ρ2∥xk+1−y+uk∥2=soft-threshold(λ/ρ,xk+1+uk)\displaystyle \begin{aligned} y^{k+1} & = \arg\min_{y} \lambda\|y\|_1 + \frac{\rho}{2}\| x^{k+1} - y + u^k\|^2 \\ & = \text{soft-threshold}(\lambda/\rho, x^{k+1} + u^k) \end{aligned}yk+1​=argymin​λ∥y∥1​+2ρ​∥xk+1−y+uk∥2=soft-threshold(λ/ρ,xk+1+uk)​

So ADMM can be interpreted as a method for solving the lasso problem by iteratively carrying out ridge regression.

Example 3 (TV-deblurring) The original problem is

min⁡x∈Rm×nμ∥Dx∥2,1+12∥Ax−x⋄∥2(6) \displaystyle \begin{aligned} \min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}} \mu \|Dx\|_{2,1} + \frac{1}{2}\|Ax-x^{\diamond}\|^2 \end{aligned} (6)x∈Rm×nmin​μ∥Dx∥2,1​+21​∥Ax−x⋄∥2​(6)

In order to apply ADMM, we need to introduce a splitting variable. We let p=Dx {p=Dx}p=Dx. The problem becomes

min⁡x,pμ∥p∥2,1+12∥Ax−x⋄∥2subject to Dx−p=0(7) \displaystyle \begin{aligned} &\min_{x,p} \mu \|p\|_{2,1} + \frac{1}{2}\|Ax-x^{\diamond}\|^2\\ &\text{subject to } Dx-p=0 \end{aligned} (7)​x,pmin​μ∥p∥2,1​+21​∥Ax−x⋄∥2subject to Dx−p=0​(7)

Then the p {p}p-subproblem can be computed by Moreau decomposition

pk+1=arg⁡min⁡pμ∥p∥2,1+ρ2∥Dxk−p+uk∥2=prox∥⋅∥2,1/ρ(Dxk+uk)=(I−μρproj{ρμ∥⋅∥2,∞=1})(Dxk+uk)\displaystyle \begin{aligned} p^{k+1} &= \arg\min_{p} \mu \|p\|_{2,1} + \frac{\rho}{2}\| Dx^{k} - p + u^k\|^2 = \text{prox}_{\|\cdot\|_{2,1}/\rho}(Dx^{k}+u^k) \\ &= (I- \frac{\mu}{\rho}\text{proj}_{\{\frac{\rho}{\mu}\|\cdot\|_{2,\infty}=1\}})(Dx^{k}+u^k) \end{aligned}pk+1​=argpmin​μ∥p∥2,1​+2ρ​∥Dxk−p+uk∥2=prox∥⋅∥2,1​/ρ​(Dxk+uk)=(I−ρμ​proj{μρ​∥⋅∥2,∞​=1}​)(Dxk+uk)​

The x {x}x-subproblem can be solved in closed form

xk+1=arg⁡min⁡x12∥Ax−x⋄∥2+ρ2∥Dx−pk+1+uk∥2=D(DTD+ATA/ρ)−1(DT(pk+1−uk)+ATu⋄/ρ)\displaystyle \begin{aligned} x^{k+1} &= \arg\min_{x} \frac{1}{2}\|Ax-x^{\diamond}\|^2 + \frac{\rho}{2}\| Dx - p^{k+1} + u^k\|^2 \\ &= D(D^TD+A^TA/\rho)^{-1}(D^T(p^{k+1}-u^k)+A^Tu^{\diamond}/\rho) \end{aligned}xk+1​=argxmin​21​∥Ax−x⋄∥2+2ρ​∥Dx−pk+1+uk∥2=D(DTD+ATA/ρ)−1(DT(pk+1−uk)+ATu⋄/ρ)​

which can be computed efficiently using FFT if periodic boundary condition is given (the above notation assumes the matrices are real-valued, otherwise one need to the use the Hermitian transpose to respect the Hermitian inner product).

And many more to be listed here...

2. Monotone inclusion problems; fixed point iterations

We mentioned in the previous post that the optimization problem can be regarded as solving for the inclusion relation

0∈∂g(x)+∂h(x),\displaystyle 0\in \partial g(x)+\partial h(x),0∈∂g(x)+∂h(x),

where ∂g(x),∂h(x) {\partial g(x),\partial h(x)}∂g(x),∂h(x) are subdifferentials of convex functions f,g {f,g}f,g. It is a inclusion relation because subdifferential operator is in general set-valued. These operators are examples of monotone operators. We often abuse the notation Ax {Ax}Ax to mean both the set or any element in it, which meaning is used should be clear from the context.

Definition 1 A set-valued operator A:Rd→2Rn {A:\mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow 2^{\mathbb{R}^n}}A:Rd→2Rn is called monotone if

⟨Ax−Ay,x−y⟩≥0,∀x,y\displaystyle \langle Ax- Ay, x-y\rangle \geq 0, \quad \forall x,y⟨Ax−Ay,x−y⟩≥0,∀x,y

Furthermore,

*- A {A}A is called maximal monotone if there does not exist a pair (x~,u~) {(\tilde{x},\tilde{u})}(x~,u~) such that u~∉Ax {\tilde{u}\notin Ax}u~∈/Ax but ⟨u~−v,x~−y⟩≥0 {\langle \tilde{u}- v, \tilde{x}-y\rangle \geq 0}⟨u~−v,x~−y⟩≥0 for all y {y}y and v∈Ay {v \in Ay}v∈Ay.

  • A {A}A is called σ {\sigma}σ-strongly monotone, or σ {\sigma}σ-coercive if the stronger inequality holds

    ⟨Ax−Ay,x−y⟩≥σ∥x−y∥2,∀x,y\displaystyle \langle Ax- Ay, x-y\rangle \geq \sigma\|x-y\|^2, \quad \forall x,y⟨Ax−Ay,x−y⟩≥σ∥x−y∥2,∀x,y *

Subdifferentials of convex functions are maximal monotone. (Actually, subdifferential can be defined for general functions, which will be monotone but need not be maximal monotone). As a result of Minty, A {A}A is maximal monotone if and only if the range of A+αI {A+\alpha I}A+αI is Rd {\mathbb{R}^d}Rd. The subdifferential of a σ {\sigma}σ-strongly convex function is σ {\sigma}σ-strongly monotone.

It turned out that a quite general convergence theory can be developed in the framework of monotone operators. To motivate, let us consider the forward-backward splitting iteration

xk+1=proxτh(xk−τ∇g(xk)),\displaystyle x^{k+1} = \text{prox}_{\tau h}(x^k-\tau \nabla g(x^k)),xk+1=proxτh​(xk−τ∇g(xk)),

where we assumed the convex functions g {g}g has L {L}L-Lipschitz gradient and ``proximability" of h {h}h. Let us write it in a more abstract form

xk+1=Jτ∂h∘Fτ∂g(xk),\displaystyle x^{k+1} = J_{\tau\partial h}\circ F_{\tau \partial g}(x^k),xk+1=Jτ∂h​∘Fτ∂g​(xk),

where Fτ∂g=I−τ∇g {F_{\tau \partial g} = I - \tau\nabla g}Fτ∂g​=I−τ∇g, Jτ∂h=(I+τ∂g)−1 {J_{\tau\partial h} = (I + \tau \partial g)^{-1}}Jτ∂h​=(I+τ∂g)−1. We showed last time that a fixed point x∗ {x^*}x∗ of this iteration satisfies the optimality condition

0∈∇g(x∗)+∂h(x∗).\displaystyle 0\in \nabla g(x^*) + \partial h(x^*).0∈∇g(x∗)+∂h(x∗).

The convergence of the algorithm thus can be modeled as the fixed point iteration of the operator Jτ∂h∘Fτ∂g {J_{\tau\partial h}\circ F_{\tau \partial g}}Jτ∂h​∘Fτ∂g​. In the following we shall present some quintessence of this theory.

2.1. Averaged operators; resolvents and reflected resolvents

Averaged operators are a class of operators that is useful for proving convergence when contractive operators are not available.

Definition 2 A set valued mapping G {G}G is called nonexpansive if

∥Gx−Gy∥≤∥x−y∥∀x,y\displaystyle \| Gx- Gy\|\leq \|x-y\| \quad \forall x,y∥Gx−Gy∥≤∥x−y∥∀x,y

In other words, G {G}G is 1 {1}1-Lipschitz continuous.

Definition 3 A set valued mapping F {F}F is called α {\alpha}α-averaged, 0<α<1 {0<\alpha<1}0<α<1, if

F=αI+(1−α)G\displaystyle F = \alpha I + (1-\alpha) GF=αI+(1−α)G

where G {G}G is a nonexpansive operator. When α=1/2 {\alpha = 1/2}α=1/2, it is often called a firmly nonexpansive operator.

Exercise 1 Show that the sets of fixed points of the operators G {G}G and F=αI+(1−α)G {F =\alpha I + (1-\alpha) G}F=αI+(1−α)G coincide.

Exercise 2 (Fundamental estimate for averaged operators) Show that F {F}F is α {\alpha}α-averaged if and only if

∥Fx−Fy∥2≤∥x−y∥2−1−αα∥(I−F)x−(I−F)y∥2\displaystyle \|Fx-Fy\|^2 \leq \|x-y\|^2 - \frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\|(I-F)x-(I-F)y\|^2∥Fx−Fy∥2≤∥x−y∥2−α1−α​∥(I−F)x−(I−F)y∥2

for all x,y {x,y}x,y. (Hint: use the fact that α−1αI−1αF {\frac{\alpha -1}{\alpha} I - \frac{1}{\alpha} F}αα−1​I−α1​F is nonexpansive.)

Now let us look at the gradient step operator Fτg {F_{\tau g}}Fτg​ for a L {L}L-Lipschitz function g {g}g.

Exercise 3 Let g {g}g be a function with L {L}L-Lipschitz gradient. Show that Fτg {F_{\tau g}}Fτg​ is max⁡{1,∣1−τL∣} {\max\{1,|1-\tau L|\}}max{1,∣1−τL∣}-Lipschitz. In particular, when 0<τ≤2/L {0<\tau \leq 2/L}0<τ≤2/L, Fτg {F_{\tau g}}Fτg​ is nonexpansive, and when 0<τ<2/L {0<\tau < 2/L}0<τ<2/L, Fτg {F_{\tau g}}Fτg​ is τL/2 {\tau L/2}τL/2-averaged, and when τ=1/L {\tau = 1/L}τ=1/L it is firmly nonexpansive. Compare this result with the descent lemma. As a consequence, we have the estimate for all x,y {x,y}x,y

∥Fτ∂g(x)−Fτ∂g(y)∥2≤∥x−y∥2−(2Lτ−1)∥(I−Fτ∂g)(x−y)∥2.\displaystyle \|F_{\tau \partial g}(x) - F_{\tau \partial g}(y)\|^2 \leq \|x -y\|^2 - (\frac{2}{L\tau}-1)\|(I-F_{\tau \partial g})(x-y)\|^2.∥Fτ∂g​(x)−Fτ∂g​(y)∥2≤∥x−y∥2−(Lτ2​−1)∥(I−Fτ∂g​)(x−y)∥2.

Note that (2Lτ−1)>0 {(\frac{2}{L\tau}-1) > 0}(Lτ2​−1)>0 if and only if 0<τ<2L {0<\tau<\frac{2}{L}}0<τ<L2​.

The above inequality is the crucial estimates for convergence of gradient descent in the setting of fixed point iteration. To see this, first we note that the distances ∥Fτ∂g(xk)−x∗∥2 {\|F_{\tau \partial g}(x^k) - x^*\|^2}∥Fτ∂g​(xk)−x∗∥2 is decreasing by our choice of τ {\tau}τ. And writing α=τL/2 {\alpha = \tau L/2}α=τL/2, with x=xk,y=x∗ {x=x^k, y=x^*}x=xk,y=x∗ we get

∥xk+1−x∗∥2≤∥xk−x∗∥2−1−αα∥(I−Fτ∂g)xk∥2=∥xk−x∗∥2−1−αα∥xk+1−xk∥2\displaystyle \begin{aligned} \|x^{k+1} - x^*\|^2 &\leq \|x^k -x^*\|^2 - \frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\|(I-F_{\tau \partial g})x^k\|^2 \\ & = \|x^k -x^*\|^2 - \frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\|x^{k+1} - x^k\|^2 \end{aligned}∥xk+1−x∗∥2​≤∥xk−x∗∥2−α1−α​∥(I−Fτ∂g​)xk∥2=∥xk−x∗∥2−α1−α​∥xk+1−xk∥2​

Rearranging,

∥xk+1−xk∥2≤α1−α(∥xk−x∗∥2−∥xk+1−x∗∥2)\displaystyle \begin{aligned} \|x^{k+1} - x^k\|^2 \leq \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}(\|x^k -x^*\|^2 - \|x^{k+1} - x^*\|^2) \end{aligned}∥xk+1−xk∥2≤1−αα​(∥xk−x∗∥2−∥xk+1−x∗∥2)​

Summing this inequality in k=0,…,N−1 {k=0,\dots,N-1}k=0,…,N−1,

∑k=0N−1∥xk+1−xk∥2≤α1−α(∥x0−x∗∥2−∥xN−x∗∥2)≤α1−α∥x0−x∗∥2\displaystyle \begin{aligned} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \|x^{k+1} - x^k\|^2 &\leq \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}(\|x^0 -x^*\|^2 - \|x^{N} - x^*\|^2) \\ & \leq \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\|x^0 -x^*\|^2 \end{aligned}k=0∑N−1​∥xk+1−xk∥2​≤1−αα​(∥x0−x∗∥2−∥xN−x∗∥2)≤1−αα​∥x0−x∗∥2​

Since the sequence is decreasing, we conclude

∥xk+1−xk∥2≤αN(1−α)∥x0−x∗∥2\displaystyle \|x^{k+1} - x^k\|^2 \leq \frac{\alpha}{N(1-\alpha)}\|x^0 -x^*\|^2∥xk+1−xk∥2≤N(1−α)α​∥x0−x∗∥2

This does not quite show the convergence of the sequence, though. But recall that if we write Fτg=(1−α)I+αG {F_{\tau g} = (1-\alpha)I + \alpha G}Fτg​=(1−α)I+αG, the fixed point of Fτg {F_{\tau g}}Fτg​ is the same with G {G}G.

∥xk+1−xk∥2=∥(1−α)xk+αGxk−xk∥2=α2∥Gxk−xk∥2\displaystyle \|x^{k+1} - x^k\|^2 = \|(1-\alpha)x^k+ \alpha Gx^k - x^k\|^2 = \alpha^2\|Gx^k - x^k\|^2∥xk+1−xk∥2=∥(1−α)xk+αGxk−xk∥2=α2∥Gxk−xk∥2

So we have

∥Gxk−xk∥2≤1Nα(1−α)∥x0−x∗∥2→0\displaystyle \|Gx^k - x^k\|^2 \leq \frac{1}{N\alpha(1-\alpha)}\|x^0 -x^*\|^2 \rightarrow 0∥Gxk−xk∥2≤Nα(1−α)1​∥x0−x∗∥2→0

i.e. xk {x^k}xk converges to a fixed point of G {G}G, with rate O(1/N) {O(1/\sqrt{N})}O(1/N​).
This argument can well be generalised to all α {\alpha}α-averaged operators. We record this result

Theorem 4 Let F {F}F be an α {\alpha}α-averaged operator on Rd {\mathbb{R}^d}Rd with non-empty set of fixed points. Then the iteration xk+1=Fxk {x^{k+1} = Fx^k}xk+1=Fxk converges to a fixed point of F {F}F.

It is useful to note that the compositions of averaged operators is again averaged (the iteration being sort of a special case). If T1 {T_1}T1​ is α1 {\alpha_1}α1​-averaged and T2 {T_2}T2​ is α2 {\alpha_2}α2​-averaged, then T1T2 {T_1T_2}T1​T2​ is θ/(1+θ) {\theta/(1+\theta)}θ/(1+θ)-averaged with

θ=α11−α1+α21−α2.\displaystyle \theta = \frac{\alpha_1}{1-\alpha_1} +\frac{\alpha_2}{1-\alpha_2}.θ=1−α1​α1​​+1−α2​α2​​.

From function properties to operator properties. It will be useful to translate the smoothness and convexity properties of the function to operator properties of its subdifferentials.
